questions.question:
You are doing a CNS examination of a patient with a spinal injury. At which of the following
sites would the distance of two-point discrimination be greatest?

suspectLines.text: For e.g., Stimulus points on the back, for instance, must be separated by at least 65 mm before they can be distinguished as separate, whereas on the fingertips two stimuli are recognized if they are separated by as little as 2 mm. The lips have the greatest acuity (two-point discrimination threshold ~ 1 mm).

questions.explanation:
The distance of two-point discrimination is greatest at the back of the scapula.

The relative tactile acuity of a given region can be determined by the two-point discrimination test. Here, calipers are used to determine the minimum distance between the two points which can be perceived as two points. Greater the density of receptors → Smaller the receptive field → More precise the localization.
For e.g., Stimulus points on the back, for instance, must be separated by at least 65 mm before they can be distinguished as separate, whereas on the fingertips two stimuli are recognized if they are separated by as little as 2 mm. The lips have the greatest acuity (two-point discrimination threshold ~ 1 mm).
Clinical significance:
Blind individuals benefit from the tactile acuity of fingertips to facilitate the ability to read Braille. The dots forming Braille symbols are separated by 2.5 mm.
Two-point discrimination is used to test the integrity of the dorsal column (medial lemniscus) system.

questions.question: Perception of normal sensory stimuli as painful is
questions.explanation:
cm ~~
Perception of normal sensory stimuli as painful is allodynia.
Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a noxious stimulus. An example of primary
hyperalgesia is the extreme sensitivity of sunburned skin, which results from sensitization of the
skin pain endings by local tissue products released due to burns — histamine, prostaglandins, and
others.
Causalgia is a type of neuropathic pain.

questions.question:
A patient with chronic pain is undergoing transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for pain
relief. What is the basis of this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) of pain relief is based on the gate theory of
pain. This method uses electrodes to activate A° and AB fibers near the injury to relieve pain.
Gate control theory operates at the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

‘The relief may result from inhibition of pain pathways (Inhibition of C fibers and A-delta fibers) in
the dorsal horn gate, by stimulation of large-diameter touch-pressure afferents(A-beta fibers). This
is called the gate-control hypothesis.
Interesting clinical application: Touching or shaking an injured area decreases the pain due to the
injury. Stimulation with an electric vibrator at the site of pain also gives some relief,
‘The same mechanism is probably responsible for the efficacy of counterirritants. Stimulation of
the skin over an area of visceral inflammation produces some relief of the pain due to the visceral
disease. The old-fashioned mustard plaster works on this principle.
